## Clone tracking

Track each infusion-product clone into the post-infusion timepoints.

**Two design points set before any testing.**

*Patient IDs differ between stages* (`031` pre vs `P031` post). `patientShort` (P01–P07) is present
in both and verified consistent, so it is the join key. Joining on `patient` would silently
return zero overlap.

*The product frequency is itself an estimate.* Each product frequency comes from ~2–4k sampled
cells, so a binomial test treating it as known is anticonservative. We use the exact conditional
(Fisher) test, which conditions on both margins and so propagates sampling error in the product
as well as the timepoint. The naive binomial is computed alongside for comparison.

Clone = patient + top-UMI TRB CDR3 nucleotide sequence. Denominators are TRB+ cells only.
Patient P06 is excluded: its product yielded 3 cells, so no frequency is estimable.

::: {.callout-important}
**Selection, not just sampling, can make a product clone absent post-infusion.** The product is
unsorted and contains untransduced T cells; post-infusion is CAR+ sorted. A clone that was never
transduced cannot appear post-infusion, and would be misread as contraction.

This is not hypothetical here. CAR RNA detection is strongly state-dependent, and the CD8
effector (GZMH+ KLRG1+) cluster — the clonally expanded compartment of the product — retains
about half the CAR detection of other cells even after matching on sequencing depth
(logistic coefficient −1.44 on cluster membership, with depth in the model). Contraction calls
for effector-phenotype clones are therefore confounded with transduction status, and the
per-clone product CAR fraction (`prod_car_frac`) is carried through so this can be inspected.
:::

```{r}
#| label: clone-setup
clone_cells <- function(o, stage) {
  cnt <- LayerData(o, assay = "RNA", layer = "counts")
  data.table(cell = colnames(o), stage = stage, pt = as.character(o$patientShort),
             time = if (stage == "pre") "product" else as.character(o$time),
             clone = fifelse(o$tcr_has_TRB, paste0(o$patientShort, "|", o$tcr_TRB1_nt), NA_character_),
             annot = as.character(o$annot), car = as.numeric(cnt["YESCAR", ] > 0))[!is.na(clone)]
}
cc <- rbind(clone_cells(pre, "pre"), clone_cells(post, "post"))

prod_n  <- cc[stage == "pre", .(prod_total = .N), by = pt]
drop_pt <- prod_n[prod_total < 100, pt]
cc <- cc[!pt %in% drop_pt]

prod <- cc[stage == "pre", .(prod_count = .N, prod_car_frac = mean(car)), by = .(pt, clone)]
prod[prod_n, prod_total := i.prod_total, on = "pt"]
prod[, prod_freq := prod_count / prod_total]

post_tp <- cc[stage == "post", .(obs = .N), by = .(pt, time, clone)]
tp_n    <- cc[stage == "post", .(tp_total = .N), by = .(pt, time)]

grid <- prod[, .(pt, clone, prod_count, prod_freq, prod_total, prod_car_frac)][
  tp_n, on = "pt", allow.cartesian = TRUE]
grid[post_tp, obs := i.obs, on = .(pt, time, clone)]
grid[is.na(obs), obs := 0L]
grid[, expected := prod_freq * tp_total]
```

Before testing, confirm the product→post overlap behaves as sampling predicts rather than
indicating a join bug:

```{r}
#| label: clone-overlap-check
found <- grid[, .(ever_found = as.integer(any(obs > 0))), by = .(pt, clone, prod_count)]
found[, .(clones = .N, pct_ever_found = round(100 * mean(ever_found), 1)),
      by = .(size = cut(prod_count, c(0, 1, 2, 4, 9, 19, Inf),
                        labels = c("1", "2", "3-4", "5-9", "10-19", "20+")))][order(size)]
```

Overlap rises from 2.1% for singleton product clones to 98% for clones of ≥20 cells, which is the
expected sampling behaviour: most product clones are seen once in ~3,000 cells and simply are not
re-sampled. This is the user-flagged depth problem, quantified.

```{r}
#| label: clone-test
a <- grid$prod_count; b <- grid$obs
m <- a + b
n <- (grid$prod_total + grid$tp_total) - m
k <- grid$tp_total
grid[, p_contract := phyper(b, m, n, k)]
grid[, p_expand   := phyper(b - 1L, m, n, k, lower.tail = FALSE)]
grid[, p_two      := pmin(1, 2 * pmin(p_contract, p_expand))]
grid[, fdr        := p.adjust(p_two, "BH")]

# Absence is informative only if a stable clone would have been seen:
# P(obs = 0 | stable) ~ exp(-expected), so expected >= 3 gives <= 5% chance of a false zero.
grid[, contraction_powered := expected >= 3]
grid[, call := fcase(
  fdr < 0.05 & obs > expected,                       "expanding",
  fdr < 0.05 & obs < expected & contraction_powered, "contracting",
  fdr >= 0.05 & contraction_powered,                 "stable",
  default = "underpowered")]

grid[, p_binom := pmin(1, 2 * pmin(pbinom(obs, tp_total, prod_freq),
                                   pbinom(obs - 1L, tp_total, prod_freq, lower.tail = FALSE)))]
grid[, fdr_binom := p.adjust(p_binom, "BH")]

grid[, .N, by = call][order(-N)]
data.table(test = c("exact conditional", "naive binomial"),
           n_sig = c(sum(grid$fdr < 0.05), sum(grid$fdr_binom < 0.05)))
```

The naive binomial returns 148 significant calls against 90 for the exact conditional — 64% more,
the anticonservatism predicted above. A concrete case: a singleton product clone observed 14 times
at a timepoint looks like a 13-fold expansion, but with one product cell the frequency is
compatible with a range that includes the observed count, and the conditional test returns
FDR 0.50. The naive test calls it significant.

```{r}
#| label: clone-test-filtered
# Independent filtering: restrict to clones whose product frequency is estimable (>=2 product
# cells). This uses ONLY the product sample, so it cannot bias the post-infusion comparison.
g2 <- grid[prod_count >= 2]
g2[, fdr_f := p.adjust(p_two, "BH")]
g2[, call_f := fcase(
  fdr_f < 0.05 & obs > expected,                       "expanding",
  fdr_f < 0.05 & obs < expected & contraction_powered, "contracting",
  fdr_f >= 0.05 & contraction_powered,                 "stable",
  default = "underpowered")]
g2[, .N, by = call_f][order(-N)]
```

**Result: 98% of clone × timepoint tests are underpowered.** In the filtered universe (3,371
tests) there are 105 contracting, 17 expanding and 623 stable calls. Expansion calls are few
because the conditional test is honest about product-frequency uncertainty, which is where most
of the apparent signal in a naive analysis comes from.

### Peak versus persistence

Peak = first timepoint in d08–d14; persistence = last in d28–d90. Four patients (P02, P04, P05,
P07) have both.

```{r}
#| label: clone-phase
tp_n[, day := as.integer(sub("^d", "", time))]
phase <- rbind(
  tp_n[day <= 14][order(pt, day)][, .SD[1], by = pt][, phase := "peak"],
  tp_n[day >= 28][order(pt, -day)][, .SD[1], by = pt][, phase := "persistence"])
both <- phase[, .N, by = pt][N == 2, pt]
ph <- phase[pt %in% both, .(pt, time, phase, tp_total)]

cl_ph <- prod[pt %in% both, .(pt, clone, prod_count, prod_freq, prod_car_frac)]
for (p in c("peak", "persistence")) {
  tt <- ph[phase == p, .(pt, time, tot = tp_total)]
  oo <- post_tp[tt, on = .(pt, time)][, .(pt, clone, o = obs)]
  cl_ph[oo, paste0("obs_", p) := i.o, on = .(pt, clone)]
  cl_ph[tt, paste0("tot_", p) := i.tot, on = "pt"]
}
cl_ph[is.na(obs_peak), obs_peak := 0L]; cl_ph[is.na(obs_persistence), obs_persistence := 0L]

A <- cl_ph$obs_peak; B <- cl_ph$obs_persistence
M <- A + B; N2 <- (cl_ph$tot_peak + cl_ph$tot_persistence) - M; K <- cl_ph$tot_persistence
cl_ph[, p_shift := pmin(1, 2 * pmin(phyper(B - 1L, M, N2, K, lower.tail = FALSE),
                                    phyper(B, M, N2, K)))]
cl_ph[, fdr_shift := p.adjust(p_shift, "BH")]
cl_ph[, f_peak := obs_peak / tot_peak][, f_pers := obs_persistence / tot_persistence]
cl_ph[, phase_class := fcase(fdr_shift < 0.05 & f_peak > f_pers, "peak-dominant",
                             fdr_shift < 0.05 & f_pers > f_peak, "persistence-dominant",
                             default = "no shift")]
dcast(cl_ph[, .N, by = .(pt, phase_class)], pt ~ phase_class, value.var = "N", fill = 0)
```

Only 9 clones shift significantly across all four patients. The reason is depth: persistence
timepoints have 360–1,178 cells.

```{r}
#| label: phase-power
cl_ph[, exp_peak := prod_freq * tot_peak][, exp_pers := prod_freq * tot_persistence]
cl_ph[, .(clones = .N,
          measurable_at_peak = sum(exp_peak >= 3),
          measurable_at_persistence = sum(exp_pers >= 3),
          measurable_at_BOTH = sum(exp_peak >= 3 & exp_pers >= 3)), by = pt][order(pt)]
```

**Only 5–26 clones per patient (45 total) are jointly measurable at both phases.**

### Testing the "different precursors" claim

The claim is that peak-dominant and persistence-dominant clones arise from different product
precursors. Rather than a low-powered binary split, we test it continuously: among jointly
measurable clones, does a clone's persistence-vs-peak bias relate to its product phenotype?
Patient is included as a covariate, because the clone sets are patient-specific.

```{r}
#| label: precursor-test
jm <- cl_ph[exp_peak >= 3 & exp_pers >= 3]
eps <- 0.5
jm[, pers_bias := log2(((obs_persistence + eps) / tot_persistence) / ((obs_peak + eps) / tot_peak))]
prod_phen <- cc[stage == "pre", .(f_mem = mean(annot == "TCF7+ CCR7+ memory (CD4/CD8)"),
                                  f_eff = mean(annot == "CD8 effector (GZMH+ KLRG1+)"),
                                  f_prolif = mean(grepl("^Prolif|^Activated prolif", annot)),
                                  f_car = mean(car)), by = .(pt, clone)]
jm <- prod_phen[jm, on = .(pt, clone)]

# Clones unobserved at BOTH phases carry no bias information; they sit at the pseudocount centre.
jm2 <- jm[obs_peak + obs_persistence > 0]
n_jm_shallow <- nrow(jm)   # used inline in the prose below
range(jm$f_mem)   # degenerate: these large clones have essentially no memory-cluster cells

jm2[, .(n = .N, rho_f_eff = round(cor(f_eff, pers_bias, method = "spearman"), 3)), by = pt][order(pt)]
c(pooled_rho_f_eff = round(cor(jm2$f_eff, jm2$pers_bias, method = "spearman"), 3),
  median_within_patient_rho = round(median(jm2[, cor(f_eff, pers_bias, method = "spearman"), by = pt]$V1), 3))

for (v in c("f_eff", "f_prolif", "f_car")) {
  fit <- summary(lm(reformulate(c(v, "pt"), "pers_bias"), data = jm2))
  cat(sprintf("%-9s beta=%7.3f  se=%6.3f  p=%.3f\n", v, coef(fit)[2,1], coef(fit)[2,2], coef(fit)[2,4]))
}
```

On this timepoint selection the claim does not reproduce: the pooled Spearman between product
effector fraction and persistence bias is 0.368, but the median *within-patient* correlation is
0.039 (Simpson's paradox), and with patient in the model no product phenotype predicts
persistence bias (f_eff p = 0.98, f_prolif p = 0.94, f_car p = 0.19). `f_mem` is degenerate —
the jointly measurable (large) product clones have essentially no memory-cluster cells.

**However, this result is partly an artefact of the timepoint rule above, which cost more power
than the data itself did.** See the next section.

### Revisiting: timepoint choice, not data depth, was the binding constraint

Two choices above were wasteful. Clone counting was restricted to GEX-QC cells, when it only
needs a productive TRB (the TCR libraries hold 7–38% more cells). And "persistence" took the
*latest* timepoint, when it should take the *deepest valid* one: for P02 that meant d90
(631 TCR cells) instead of d28 (5,609) — a 9× loss. The peak rule had the same flaw, selecting
near-empty d05 libraries (P49 peak = 1 cell).

Re-selecting the **deepest library within each window** (peak d08–d14, persistence ≥d28), and
counting from the TCR libraries directly:

```{r}
#| label: power-recoverable
ct <- fread(geo_file("All_TCR_Aggregated_filtered_contig_annotations.csv.gz"),
            select = c("barcode", "origin", "chain", "cdr3_nt", "umis", "donor", "Meta:time"))
setnames(ct, "Meta:time", "time")
tb <- ct[chain == "TRB" & umis >= 2][order(barcode, -umis)][, .SD[1], by = barcode]
tb[, pt := paste0("P", donor)][, clone := paste0(pt, "|", cdr3_nt)]

prodT <- tb[time == "d00", .(prod_count = .N), by = .(pt, clone)]
prodT[tb[time == "d00", .(prod_total = .N), by = pt], prod_total := i.prod_total, on = "pt"]
prodT[, prod_freq := prod_count / prod_total]
postT <- tb[time != "d00"]
tpT   <- postT[, .(tot = .N), by = .(pt, time)][, day := as.integer(sub("d", "", time))]

pick2 <- rbind(
  tpT[day >= 8 & day <= 14][order(pt, -tot)][, .SD[1], by = pt][, phase := "peak"],
  tpT[day >= 28][order(pt, -tot)][, .SD[1], by = pt][, phase := "persistence"])
pick2[order(pt, phase)]

# jointly measurable clones under this (deepest-library) selection
both2 <- pick2[, .N, by = pt][N == 2, pt]
res2  <- prodT[pt %in% both2]
cnt2  <- postT[pt %in% both2, .N, by = .(pt, time, clone)]
for (ph2 in c("peak", "persistence")) {
  sl <- pick2[phase == ph2 & pt %in% both2, .(pt, time, tot)]
  res2[cnt2[sl, on = .(pt, time)], paste0("obs_", ph2) := i.N, on = .(pt, clone)]
  res2[sl, paste0("tot_", ph2) := i.tot, on = "pt"]
}
res2[is.na(obs_peak), obs_peak := 0L]; res2[is.na(obs_persistence), obs_persistence := 0L]
n_jm_deep <- res2[prod_freq * tot_peak >= 3 & prod_freq * tot_persistence >= 3, .N]
n_jm_deep
```

This more than doubles the jointly measurable set, to **`r n_jm_deep` clones** (from `r n_jm_shallow`); P49 alone goes from
0 to 67 once both of its timepoints are deep.

Re-testing the claim on that set (43 clones with product phenotype, 4 patients) **changes the
answer**:

| Predictor | Previous (45-clone set) | Deepest-timepoint set |
|---|---|---|
| f_eff (product effector fraction) | p = 0.98, within-patient rho 0.039 | p = 0.119, within-patient rho **0.228** |
| f_prolif | p = 0.94 | p = 0.649 |
| f_car (product CAR fraction) | p = 0.19 | beta = −4.85, **p = 0.001** |

So there *is* a signal: clones with lower product CAR fraction are more persistence-biased, and
effector-phenotype product clones trend toward persistence bias — the opposite direction to the
usual "memory precursors persist" expectation.

::: {.callout-warning}
**Do not read the `f_car` result as biology yet.** Product CAR detection is confounded with cell
state and depth (see the earlier callout): low-CAR product cells are enriched in the CD8 effector
cluster, so `f_car` and `f_eff` are negatively correlated and point the same way here. The
association is equally consistent with (a) genuine biology — lower CAR expression means less
tonic signalling and better persistence, which is established CAR-T biology — and (b) the
effector-phenotype signal re-expressed through a confounded proxy. These cannot be separated
with this data.
:::

**Why more sequencing would not settle it.** The limiting factor is not depth. Among well-measured
clones, 90% in P02 and 86% in P06 are absent at *both* post-infusion phases. Those clones are
uninformative about phase bias, and their absence is confounded with transduction status, since
the product is unsorted and post-infusion is CAR+ sorted. Deeper sequencing of the same libraries
would not change that — it is a selection effect, not a sampling one. What would resolve it:
bulk TCR-seq on the same samples, or the endogenous CD3+CAR− libraries.

## Three-phase trajectory (expansion / persistence 1 / persistence 2)

The two-phase framing above is wrong: the authors use **three** phases. The sampling structure
makes the intended design obvious — every patient has a d21 timepoint, which the binary analysis
discarded entirely (20,593 cells, and the *deepest* timepoint for three patients).

Phase definitions are the authors' own (study schematic): **T_exp d8–12, T_per1 d21, T_per2 d28**,
with the infusion product (IP) as the baseline. Cells were sorted CD3+ CD19-tetramer+.

Two patients were drawn off schedule, and the deposited data has extra samples outside the
three-phase design:

| Deviation | Handling |
|---|---|
| P04 T_per2 drawn d30, not d28 | kept as T_per2 (schedule slippage) |
| P06 T_exp drawn d14, outside d8–12 | moot — P06 excluded anyway (7 product cells) |
| P02 d90, P02/P03 d05 | excluded; not part of the three-phase design |

After this, every analysed patient (P01, P02, P04, P05, P07) sits inside the authors' windows.

::: {.callout-note}
**All 7 patients are complete responders.** There is no responder / non-responder contrast in
this dataset, so nothing here can link a clone's persistence to clinical outcome — the question
is only what distinguishes persistent clones *within* responders.
:::

```{r}
#| label: three-phase-structure
ct <- fread(geo_file("All_TCR_Aggregated_filtered_contig_annotations.csv.gz"),
            select = c("barcode", "chain", "cdr3_nt", "umis", "donor", "Meta:time"))
setnames(ct, "Meta:time", "time")
tb <- ct[chain == "TRB" & umis >= 2][order(barcode, -umis)][, .SD[1], by = barcode]
dmap <- c(`31` = "P04", `33` = "P01", `34` = "P03", `39` = "P05", `48` = "P06", `49` = "P02", `116` = "P07")
tb[, pt := dmap[as.character(donor)]][, clone := paste0(pt, "|", cdr3_nt)]
tb[, day := as.integer(sub("d", "", time))]
dcast(tb[, .N, by = .(pt, day)], pt ~ day, value.var = "N", fill = 0)[order(pt)]

# Authors' windows: T_exp d8-12, T_per1 d21, T_per2 d28 (d30 kept as P04's T_per2).
tb[, phase := fcase(day == 0, "product", day >= 8 & day <= 14, "expansion",
                    day == 21, "persistence1", day >= 28 & day <= 30, "persistence2")]
tbp <- tb[!is.na(phase)]
# Confirm every analysed patient-day falls in an authors' window
tbp[phase != "product", sort(unique(day))]
```

Rather than a single ratio, fit each clone a **trajectory**: weighted least squares of log
frequency on phase index, using whichever phases are measurable for that clone (expected ≥ 3,
at least two phases), weighted by observed count. A negative slope means the clone declines
across the phases; positive means it is maintained or rises.

```{r}
#| label: trajectory-fit
prodP <- tbp[phase == "product", .(prod_count = .N), by = .(pt, clone)]
prodP[tbp[phase == "product", .(prod_total = .N), by = pt], prod_total := i.prod_total, on = "pt"]
prodP[, prod_freq := prod_count / prod_total]
keep_pt <- prodP[, .(tot = max(prod_total)), by = pt][tot >= 100, pt]
tot3 <- tbp[phase != "product", .(tot = .N), by = .(pt, phase)]
use  <- intersect(keep_pt, tot3[, .N, by = pt][N == 3, pt])

cnt3 <- tbp[phase != "product" & pt %in% use, .N, by = .(pt, phase, clone)]
gr <- prodP[pt %in% use][tot3[pt %in% use], on = "pt", allow.cartesian = TRUE]
gr[cnt3, obs := i.N, on = .(pt, phase, clone)]
gr[is.na(obs), obs := 0L]
gr[, expected := prod_freq * tot][, pidx := match(phase, c("expansion", "persistence1", "persistence2"))]

gm  <- gr[expected >= 3]
ok2 <- gm[, .N, by = .(pt, clone)][N >= 2]
gm  <- gm[ok2[, .(pt, clone)], on = .(pt, clone)]
gm[, `:=`(y = log((obs + 0.5) / tot), w = obs + 0.5)]
slopes <- gm[, { f <- lm(y ~ pidx, weights = w)
                 .(slope = unname(coef(f)[2]), n_phase = .N, tot_obs = sum(obs)) }, by = .(pt, clone)]
slopes <- prodP[slopes, on = .(pt, clone)]
slopes[, .(clones = .N, informative = sum(tot_obs > 0)), by = pt][order(pt)]
```

138 clones get a trajectory across 5 patients; 76 also have a product phenotype.

```{r}
#| label: trajectory-test
cnt_pre <- LayerData(pre, assay = "RNA", layer = "counts")
pp <- data.table(clone = paste0(as.character(pre$patientShort), "|", pre$tcr_TRB1_nt),
                 has = pre$tcr_has_TRB, annot = as.character(pre$annot),
                 umi = pre$nCount_RNA, car = as.numeric(cnt_pre["YESCAR", ] > 0))[has == TRUE]
pp <- pp[, .(n_gex = .N, med_umi = median(umi),
             f_eff = mean(annot == "CD8 effector (GZMH+ KLRG1+)"),
             f_mem = mean(annot == "TCF7+ CCR7+ memory (CD4/CD8)"),
             f_prolif = mean(grepl("^Prolif|^Activated prolif", annot)),
             f_car = mean(car)), by = clone]
sl2 <- pp[slopes[tot_obs > 0], on = "clone"][!is.na(f_eff)][, log_umi := log10(med_umi)]

for (v in c("f_eff", "f_mem", "f_prolif", "f_car")) {
  fit <- summary(lm(reformulate(c(v, "pt"), "slope"), data = sl2))
  cat(sprintf("%-9s beta=%7.3f  p=%.4f\n", v, coef(fit)[2,1], coef(fit)[2,4]))
}
car_fit <- coef(summary(lm(slope ~ f_car + pt, data = sl2)))
car_beta <- car_fit["f_car", 1]
car_p <- car_fit["f_car", 4]
```

### Result

**Product differentiation state does not predict the trajectory.** Effector fraction p = 0.34,
memory fraction p = 0.22, proliferating fraction p = 0.72. On this data the "different
precursors" claim does not reproduce when precursor is defined by differentiation phenotype —
and unlike the two-phase attempt, `f_mem` is now testable rather than degenerate.

**Product CAR expression does predict it, but the result is fragile.** Lower product CAR fraction
goes with better maintenance (beta = `r sprintf('%.2f', car_beta)`, p = `r sprintf('%.4f', car_p)`), and unlike the earlier effector signal
this holds *within* patients (median rho −0.42), so it is not Simpson's paradox. It also survives
adjustment for effector phenotype and product sequencing depth:

```{r}
#| label: car-confound-adjust
for (f in list(slope ~ f_car + pt, slope ~ f_car + f_eff + pt, slope ~ f_car + log_umi + pt,
               slope ~ f_car + f_eff + log_umi + pt)) {
  co <- coef(summary(lm(f, sl2)))
  cat(sprintf("%-42s f_car beta=%7.3f  p=%.4f\n", deparse(f), co["f_car",1], co["f_car",4]))
}
sl2[, .(clones = .N, median_slope = round(median(slope), 2), pct_rising = round(100 * mean(slope > 0))),
    by = .(car_bin = cut(f_car, c(-.01, .1, .3, .5, 1)))][order(car_bin)]
```

There is a clean dose-response — median slope falls 0.69 → 0.49 → 0.13 → 0.10 and the share of
rising clones falls 94% → 85% → 71% → 58% across increasing product CAR fraction — which argues
for something real.

## Linking fate to product phenotype

Map fate-classified clones back to their infusion-product cells. Clones are split by trajectory
slope into **expansion-biased** (bottom tertile, least maintained) and **persistence-biased**
(top tertile). Note this is a relative gradient, not "expands then vanishes" versus "persists":
the median slope of the expansion-biased group is −0.16, i.e. nearly flat.

This section is self-contained: it rebuilds clone counts and fate classes from the TCR libraries
so it does not depend on objects cleaned up earlier.

```{r}
#| label: fate-rebuild
ct <- fread(geo_file("All_TCR_Aggregated_filtered_contig_annotations.csv.gz"),
            select = c("barcode", "chain", "cdr3_nt", "umis", "donor", "Meta:time"))
setnames(ct, "Meta:time", "time")
tb <- ct[chain == "TRB" & umis >= 2][order(barcode, -umis)][, .SD[1], by = barcode]
dmap <- c(`31`="P04", `33`="P01", `34`="P03", `39`="P05", `48`="P06", `49`="P02", `116`="P07")
tb[, pt := dmap[as.character(donor)]][, clone := paste0(pt, "|", cdr3_nt)][, day := as.integer(sub("d","",time))]
tb[, phase := fcase(day == 0, "IP", day >= 8 & day <= 14, "T_exp",
                    day == 21, "T_per1", day >= 28 & day <= 30, "T_per2")]
tbp <- tb[!is.na(phase)][, phase := factor(phase, levels = c("IP","T_exp","T_per1","T_per2"))]

ptot <- tbp[, .(tot = .N), by = .(pt, phase)]
use  <- intersect(ptot[, .N, by = pt][N == 4, pt], ptot[phase == "IP" & tot >= 100, pt])
cnt  <- ptot[tbp[pt %in% use, .N, by = .(pt, phase, clone)], on = .(pt, phase)][, freq := N / tot]

w <- dcast(cnt, pt + clone ~ phase, value.var = "N", fill = 0)
w <- ptot[phase == "IP", .(pt, tot_IP = tot)][w, on = "pt"][, prod_freq := IP / tot_IP]
for (p in c("T_exp","T_per1","T_per2")) w[ptot[phase == p], (paste0("tot_", p)) := i.tot, on = "pt"]
long <- melt(w[, .(pt, clone, prod_freq, T_exp, T_per1, T_per2, tot_T_exp, tot_T_per1, tot_T_per2)],
             id.vars = c("pt","clone","prod_freq"), measure.vars = patterns("^T_", "^tot_T"),
             variable.name = "pidx", value.name = c("obs","tot"))
long[, pidx := as.integer(pidx)][, expected := prod_freq * tot]
lm2 <- long[expected >= 3]
lm2 <- lm2[lm2[, .N, by = .(pt, clone)][N >= 2][, .(pt, clone)], on = .(pt, clone)]
lm2[, `:=`(y = log((obs + 0.5) / tot), ww = obs + 0.5)]
slopes <- lm2[, { f <- lm(y ~ pidx, weights = ww)
                  .(slope = unname(coef(f)[2]), tot_obs = sum(obs)) }, by = .(pt, clone)][tot_obs > 0]
slopes[, fate := fcase(slope <= quantile(slope, 1/3), "Expansion-biased",
                       slope >= quantile(slope, 2/3), "Persistence-biased", default = "Intermediate")]
cnt <- slopes[, .(pt, clone, fate)][cnt, on = .(pt, clone)][is.na(fate), fate := "Not tracked"]
slopes[, .N, by = fate]
```

```{r}
#| label: fate-to-cluster
# Fisher OR per product cluster, cell level. OR > 1 = enriched in persistence-biased clones.
pc <- data.table(clone = paste0(as.character(pre$patientShort), "|", pre$tcr_TRB1_nt),
                 has = pre$tcr_has_TRB, annot = as.character(pre$annot),
                 pt = as.character(pre$patientShort))[has == TRUE][, idx := .I]
pc <- slopes[, .(clone, fate)][pc, on = "clone"][fate %in% c("Expansion-biased", "Persistence-biased")]
pc[, fate2 := fifelse(fate == "Persistence-biased", "pers", "exp")]

ors <- rbindlist(lapply(unique(pc$annot), function(cl) {
  a <- pc[fate2=="pers" & annot==cl, .N]; b <- pc[fate2=="pers" & annot!=cl, .N]
  cc <- pc[fate2=="exp" & annot==cl, .N]; d <- pc[fate2=="exp" & annot!=cl, .N]
  ft <- fisher.test(matrix(c(a, b, cc, d), 2, byrow = TRUE))
  data.table(cluster = cl, n_pers = a, n_exp = cc, OR = unname(ft$estimate),
             lo = ft$conf.int[1], hi = ft$conf.int[2], p_cell = ft$p.value) }))
ors[, fdr_cell := p.adjust(p_cell, "BH")]
ors[order(-OR), .(cluster, n_pers, n_exp, OR = round(OR, 2),
                  CI = paste0(round(lo,2), "-", round(hi,2)), fdr = signif(fdr_cell, 2))]
or_eff  <- ors[cluster == "CD8 effector (GZMH+ KLRG1+)", OR]
fdr_eff <- ors[cluster == "CD8 effector (GZMH+ KLRG1+)", fdr_cell]
or_tc2  <- ors[cluster == "CD8 Tc2-like (GATA3+ PTGDR2+)", OR]
fdr_tc2 <- ors[cluster == "CD8 Tc2-like (GATA3+ PTGDR2+)", fdr_cell]

# clone-level test (one observation per clone, patient-adjusted)
cf <- pc[, .(n = .N), by = .(clone, pt, fate2, annot)]
tc <- pc[, .(tot = .N), by = .(clone, pt, fate2)]
cf <- tc[cf, on = .(clone, pt, fate2)][, frac := n / tot]
fullc <- CJ(clone = tc$clone, annot = unique(pc$annot), unique = TRUE)
fullc <- tc[fullc, on = "clone"][cf[, .(clone, annot, frac)], on = .(clone, annot)]
fullc[is.na(frac), frac := 0]
ors[, p_clone := sapply(cluster, function(cl) {
  s <- fullc[annot == cl]; if (s[, uniqueN(frac)] < 3) return(NA_real_)
  coef(summary(lm(frac ~ fate2 + pt, data = s)))["fate2pers", 4] })]
pclone_eff <- ors[cluster == "CD8 effector (GZMH+ KLRG1+)", p_clone]
```

Cell-level, the result looks emphatic: CD8 effector (GZMH+ KLRG1+) enriched in persistence-biased
clones (OR `r sprintf('%.2f', or_eff)`, FDR `r fmt_e(fdr_eff)`) and CD8 Tc2-like (GATA3+ PTGDR2+) strongly depleted
(OR `r sprintf('%.2f', or_tc2)`, FDR `r fmt_e(fdr_tc2)`).

::: {.callout-important}
**None of it survives.** Two problems with the cell-level test:

1. **Pseudoreplication.** Cells within a clone are not independent — they are clonal descendants.
   A cluster's apparent enrichment can come from one or two large clones. The CD8 effector
   signal rests on 13 expansion-biased versus 23 persistence-biased clones.
2. **Patient confounding.** Fate class is unbalanced across patients (P04: 1 expansion-biased
   versus 10 persistence-biased; P02: 5 versus 1), and 61 of the 94 Tc2-like cells come from
   a single patient.

Re-testing at the clone level (one observation per clone) with patient adjustment:

```{r}
#| label: cell-vs-clone-level
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(
  ors[n_pers + n_exp >= 20][order(-OR),
      .(Cluster = cluster, `Cell-level FDR` = fmt_e(fdr_cell),
        `Clone-level p (patient-adjusted)` = sprintf("%.3f", p_clone))],
  caption = "Cell-level significance vs the clone-level test that supersedes it.")
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: fate-adjusted
# Clone-level, patient-adjusted, across product clusters + RNA markers + CITE-seq proteins

eff_g <- c("GZMK","NKG7","KLRG1","GZMH","PRF1"); mem_g <- c("TCF7","CCR7","SELL","LEF1","IL7R")
prot  <- c("CD45RA","CD45RO","CCR7","CD27","CD28","CD95","CD57")   # CD62L not in the 31-plex panel
lg <- LayerData(pre, assay = "RNA", layer = "data"); ap <- LayerData(pre, assay = "ADT", layer = "data")
pcx <- copy(pc)
for (g in c(eff_g, mem_g)) pcx[, (g) := lg[g, idx]]
for (q in prot) pcx[, (paste0("prot_", q)) := ap[q, idx]]
cm <- pcx[, lapply(.SD, mean), by = .(clone, pt, fate2), .SDcols = c(eff_g, mem_g)]
cp <- pcx[, lapply(.SD, mean), by = .(clone, pt, fate2), .SDcols = paste0("prot_", prot)]

gather <- function(vars, dat, label) rbindlist(lapply(vars, function(v) {
  co <- coef(summary(lm(reformulate(c("fate2","pt"), v), data = dat)))
  data.table(domain = label, feature = v, beta_pers = co["fate2pers",1], p = co["fate2pers",4]) }))
allres <- rbindlist(list(
  ors[!is.na(p_clone), .(domain = "product cluster", feature = cluster, beta_pers = NA_real_, p = p_clone)],
  gather(c(eff_g, mem_g), cm, "RNA marker"),
  gather(paste0("prot_", prot), cp, "CITE-seq protein")))
allres[, fdr := p.adjust(p, "BH")]
allres[order(p)][1:10, .(domain, feature, p = signif(p, 3), fdr = signif(fdr, 3))]
allres[fdr < 0.05, .N]
```

**Nothing is significant after BH across all 24 tests.** The requested effector-versus-memory
contrast (GZMK, NKG7, KLRG1 against TCF7, CCR7, SELL) shows no patient-adjusted difference: all
effector markers trend *lower* in persistence-biased clones (GZMK p = 0.14, others p > 0.33) and
all memory markers show raw means higher in persistence-biased clones but lose it entirely on
patient adjustment (TCF7 p = 0.75, CCR7 p = 0.89, SELL p = 0.78) — another between-patient effect.

CITE-seq proteins agree. CD62L is not in the 31-plex panel, so memory state rests on CD45RA,
CD45RO, CCR7, CD27, CD28, CD95. The only nominal hit is **CD57 lower in persistence-biased clones**
(beta −0.134, p = 0.021), which is biologically coherent — CD57 marks terminal differentiation —
but it does not survive correction (FDR 0.49) and is one of seven proteins tested.

::: {.callout-warning}
**A structural limit, not just a power limit.** The memory clusters are essentially absent from
fate-classifiable clones: the TCF7+ CCR7+ memory cluster contributes **1 cell** and CD4 memory
**3 cells**, against hundreds in the effector and proliferating clusters. Clones large enough to
track reliably are, by construction, the clonally expanded ones — and those are effector and
proliferating, not memory. So the memory-precursor hypothesis cannot be tested in this design at
all, whatever the sample size. Testing it needs clone tracking that does not condition on product
abundance, i.e. bulk TCR-seq.
:::

### Plots

```{r}
#| label: plot-alluvial
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 7
library(ggalluvial)
topn <- cnt[, .(mx = max(freq)), by = .(pt, clone)][order(pt, -mx)][, head(.SD, 10), by = pt]
al <- cnt[topn[, .(pt, clone)], on = .(pt, clone)]
al <- al[CJ(pt = unique(al$pt), clone = unique(al$clone), phase = levels(cnt$phase), unique = TRUE),
         on = .(pt, clone, phase)][topn[, .(pt, clone)], on = .(pt, clone)]
al[is.na(freq), freq := 0]
al[, fate := fate[!is.na(fate)][1], by = .(pt, clone)]
al[is.na(fate), fate := "Not tracked"]
al[, fate := factor(fate, levels = c("Expansion-biased", "Intermediate", "Persistence-biased", "Not tracked"))]

fate_cols <- c("Expansion-biased" = "#eb6834", "Intermediate" = "#b8b7b1",
               "Persistence-biased" = "#2a78d6", "Not tracked" = "#dcdbd6")
ggplot(al, aes(x = phase, y = freq, alluvium = clone, fill = fate)) +
  geom_alluvium(aes(group = clone), width = 0.3, alpha = 0.85, decreasing = FALSE,
                colour = "#fcfcfb", linewidth = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ pt, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = fate_cols, name = NULL, drop = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(title = "Top 10 clones per patient tracked across phases",
       subtitle = "Infusion product → expansion (d8–12) → persistence 1 (d21) → persistence 2 (d28)",
       x = NULL, y = "Clone frequency (of TRB+ cells)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = element_line(colour = "#ebeae6", linewidth = 0.3),
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, colour = "#52514e"),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"), legend.position = "bottom")
```

::: {.callout-important}
**The alluvial exposes a selection bias in the fate classification.** The pale "Not tracked"
clones are those with **zero** post-infusion observations at every phase — clones that vanish
completely. In P02 these include product clones of 43, 29, 19 and 18 cells that are never seen
again. A trajectory slope cannot be fitted to all zeros, so the `tot_obs > 0` filter silently
drops them.

The clones with the most dramatic fate are therefore **excluded from the expansion-versus-
persistence comparison**, and their disappearance is confounded with transduction status (the
product is unsorted, post-infusion is CAR+ sorted). Any statement about what distinguishes
persistent clones applies only to clones that survived detectably at all.
:::

```{r}
#| label: plot-or
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
od <- ors[n_pers + n_exp >= 20][order(OR)]
od[, cluster := factor(cluster, levels = cluster)]
od[, dir := fifelse(OR > 1, "Enriched in persistence-biased", "Enriched in expansion-biased")]
od[, lab := sprintf("cell FDR %s   |   clone-level p = %.2f",
                    ifelse(fdr_cell < 1e-3, format(fdr_cell, digits = 1, scientific = TRUE),
                           sprintf("%.3f", fdr_cell)), p_clone)]
ggplot(od, aes(x = log2(OR), y = cluster, fill = dir)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#52514e", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = log2(lo), xmax = log2(hi)), width = 0.18,
                colour = "#52514e", linewidth = 0.4, orientation = "y") +
  geom_text(aes(label = lab), x = 3.1, hjust = 0, size = 2.9, colour = "#52514e") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Enriched in persistence-biased" = "#2a78d6",
                               "Enriched in expansion-biased"   = "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-3,-2,-1,0,1), labels = function(x) round(2^x, 2),
                     limits = c(-4.6, 8.6)) +
  labs(title = "Infusion-product cluster enrichment by clone fate",
       subtitle = paste("Cell-level Fisher odds ratio (95% CI), persistence- vs expansion-biased clones.",
                        "\nNo cluster survives clone-level testing with patient adjustment."),
       x = "Odds ratio (log scale)", y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.x = element_line(colour = "#ebeae6", linewidth = 0.3),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"), plot.title.position = "plot",
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "#52514e", size = 8.5, lineheight = 1.2),
        legend.position = "bottom")
```

Each bar carries both verdicts deliberately: the cell-level FDR a naive analysis would report,
and the clone-level patient-adjusted p-value that supersedes it. The CD8 effector bar
(OR `r sprintf('%.2f', or_eff)`, cell FDR `r fmt_e(fdr_eff)`, clone-level p = `r sprintf('%.2f', pclone_eff)`) is the clearest case of the gap.

Figures are written to `figures/`.

::: {.callout-warning}
**But it attenuates under stricter measurement filters**: restricting to better-observed clones
gives p = 0.0012 (n = 76) → 0.099 (n = 48) → 0.109 (n = 34) → 0.83 (n = 23). The effect size
stays negative and similar in the middle strata, so this is consistent with power loss rather
than artefact, but it is not robust enough to call established. Treat as a hypothesis: lower CAR
expression → less tonic signalling → better persistence is known CAR-T biology, and this data is
consistent with it, but 76 clones in 5 patients cannot establish it.
:::

```{r}
#| label: clone-save
#| cache: false
fwrite(grid[, .(pt, time, clone, prod_count, prod_freq, prod_car_frac, tp_total, obs,
                expected, p_two, fdr, contraction_powered, call)],
       file.path(proc_dir, "clone_tracking.csv.gz"))
fwrite(cl_ph[, .(pt, clone, prod_count, prod_freq, obs_peak, tot_peak, obs_persistence,
                 tot_persistence, p_shift, fdr_shift, phase_class)],
       file.path(proc_dir, "clone_phase_shift.csv.gz"))
rm(grid, g2, cl_ph, jm, jm2, prod, prod_phen, post_tp, tp_n, phase, ph, cc, prod_n, found,
   drop_pt, both, a, b, m, n, k, A, B, M, N2, K, eps, p, v, tt, oo, fit)
invisible(gc())
```
